variants.stem: During inhalation, what does the diaphragm do?
Which change in the diaphragm allows the thoracic cavity to enlarge so that air enters the lungs?
According to Boyle's law, inspiration occurs when the volume of the thoracic cavity does what, causing lung pressure to fall below atmospheric pressure?
Which muscles contract to increase the volume of the thoracic cavity during quiet inspiration?
Air flows into the lungs when intrapleural pressure drops. Which action causes this drop?
The dome-shaped muscle separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities moves downward during which phase of breathing?
When the diaphragm contracts, which of the following occurs?
opts: The chest cavity enlarges and air is drawn in
The chest cavity shrinks and air is pushed out
The lungs shrink and air is drawn in
The ribs lower and air is drawn in

variants.stem: In negative-pressure breathing, lung pressure becomes lower than atmospheric pressure when the diaphragm:

questions.why: When the diaphragm and external intercostals contract, the thoracic cavity gets larger, pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in (inspiration).
questions.deep: Boyle's law: pressure and volume of a gas are inversely related. Inhalation = diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs lift, volume up, pressure down. Exhalation (quiet) = muscles relax, volume down, pressure up, air flows out.

variants.stem: Where does gas exchange between the air and the blood occur in the lungs?
Oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out across the walls of which tiny sacs?
Which lung structure is surrounded by capillaries and is the site of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange?
The thin-walled air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles are called:
Which structure provides the large surface area in the lungs needed for diffusion of gases?
Emphysema destroys the walls of which structures, reducing the surface available for gas exchange?
Which part of the respiratory system has walls only one cell thick so gases can diffuse easily?
Blood in the pulmonary capillaries picks up oxygen in which structures?

questions.why: Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli, tiny thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries, where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it by diffusion.
questions.deep: Air path: nose or mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary bronchi → tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. Only the alveoli are thin enough for gas exchange; the other passages just conduct air.

variants.stem: On an ECG, which complex represents depolarization of the ventricles?
Which part of the ECG corresponds to the Purkinje fibers stimulating the ventricles to contract?
Which ECG feature records ventricular depolarization, the electrical event that triggers ventricular contraction?
The P wave shows atrial depolarization. Which ECG feature shows ventricular depolarization?
Which waveform is the largest and sharpest on a normal ECG, made up of the Q, R, and S waves?
Which ECG component indicates that the ventricles have been depolarized?
A widened or abnormal version of which ECG complex may suggest abnormal conduction in the ventricles?
The T wave represents ventricular repolarization. Which ECG complex represents ventricular depolarization?

questions.why: The QRS complex records depolarization of the ventricles, which triggers ventricular contraction.
questions.deep: ECG order: P wave (atrial depolarization) → PR segment (AV node delay) → QRS complex (ventricular depolarization) → ST segment → T wave (ventricular repolarization). Atrial repolarization is hidden within the QRS complex.

variants.stem: Which ABO blood type has neither A nor B antigens on its red blood cells?
A person's red blood cells carry no A or B antigen. What is the person's ABO blood type?
Which blood type produces both anti-A and anti-B antibodies?
Which ABO type lacks both antigens on its red blood cells and has both antibodies in its plasma?
Type AB blood has both A and B antigens. Which type has neither?
Whose plasma would attack red blood cells carrying either A or B antigens?
Which ABO type has red blood cells without A or B surface antigens?
If a blood sample does not clump with anti-A serum or anti-B serum, the ABO blood type is:

questions.why: Type O red blood cells have neither A nor B antigens, and type O plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
questions.deep: Type A: A antigens, anti-B antibodies. Type B: B antigens, anti-A antibodies. Type AB: both antigens, no antibodies. Type O: no antigens, both antibodies. Rh factor is a separate antigen, giving positive or negative types.

variants.stem: Which layer of the skin contains hair follicles, sweat glands, nerve endings, and blood vessels?
Which skin layer lies directly beneath the epidermis and is made mostly of connective tissue?
The sebaceous (oil) glands and hair roots are located in which skin layer?
The epidermis has no blood vessels of its own. Which layer supplies it with nutrients?
Collagen and elastin fibers that give skin strength and elasticity are found mainly in which layer?
Touch receptors and pain receptors of the skin are located mainly in which layer?
Which is the thick, middle layer of the skin?
Sweat glands originate in which layer of the skin?

questions.why: The dermis is the thick, connective tissue layer beneath the epidermis that contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles, and sweat and oil glands.
questions.deep: Skin has three layers: epidermis (outermost, no blood vessels, keratinocytes divide in the stratum basale), dermis (middle), and hypodermis (deepest, fat and connective tissue). Skin helps with protection, thermoregulation, and sensation.

variants.stem: In anatomical position, the hip is ____ to the knee.
Which term means closer to the center of the body or to a limb's point of attachment?
The elbow is ____ to the wrist.
Which directional term describes the shoulder relative to the hand?
Which term is the opposite of distal?
The thigh is ____ to the ankle.
Which term correctly describes the position of the knee relative to the foot?
A structure nearer to the trunk than another structure on the same limb is described as:

questions.why: Proximal means closer to the center of the body or a limb's attachment point, so the hip is proximal to the knee.
questions.deep: Proximal vs distal: nearer to vs farther from the trunk or point of origin. Medial vs lateral: toward vs away from the midline. Anterior vs posterior: front vs back. Superior vs inferior: toward the head vs toward the feet. Memory aid: Proximal = Probably close.

variants.stem: Which organ produces bile?
Bile is made in one organ and stored in another. Which organ makes it?
The gallbladder stores bile. Which organ synthesizes it?
Which organ secretes the fluid that emulsifies fats in the small intestine?
Hepatocytes are the cells that make bile. In which organ are they found?
Which organ is the source of the bile salts that aid in fat digestion?
Which organ makes the greenish-yellow digestive fluid that travels through the common bile duct?
Where is bile manufactured before it is stored in the gallbladder?

questions.why: The liver produces bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder and released into the duodenum to emulsify fats.
questions.deep: Liver = makes bile. Gallbladder = stores bile. Pancreas = makes digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, proteases) and bicarbonate. Bile does not chemically digest fat; it breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones so lipase can work.

variants.stem: Which muscle type is involuntary and lacks striations?
Which muscle tissue lines the walls of the stomach, intestines, and blood vessels?
In which muscle type are actin and myosin filaments disorganized, with no sarcomeres present?
Which muscle type moves food through the digestive tract by peristalsis?
Muscle that contracts without conscious control and has no striped pattern under a microscope is:
Which muscle is found in the walls of the bladder and uterus?
Which muscle tissue lacks sarcomeres?
Which type of muscle regulates the diameter of blood vessels and airways without conscious control?

questions.why: Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated, with disorganized actin and myosin filaments and no sarcomeres.
questions.deep: Skeletal: voluntary, striated, attached to bones. Cardiac: involuntary, striated, found only in the heart. Smooth: involuntary, not striated, found in the walls of hollow organs and vessels. Both skeletal and cardiac muscle have sarcomeres.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Through which structures does inhaled air pass on its way to the alveoli?
Select all that apply: Which of these are part of the airway between the larynx and the alveoli?
Select all that apply: Which structures carry air rather than blood or food?
Select all that apply: Which are branches of the bronchial tree?
Select all that apply: Air moving into the lungs travels through which of the following?
Select all that apply: Which structures are conducting airways that lead to the alveoli?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are NOT part of the respiratory tree?
Select all that apply: Which structures does air travel through after the trachea?

questions.why: Inhaled air passes through the trachea, bronchi (primary, secondary, tertiary), and bronchioles to reach the alveoli. The esophagus, aorta, veins, and other organs belong to other systems.
questions.deep: Air path: nose or mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary bronchi → tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The esophagus lies behind the trachea and carries food, not air.

variants.stem: Tap the urinary bladder.
Tap the organ that stores urine until it is released.
Tap the muscular sac that receives urine from both ureters.
Tap the structure where the two ureters empty.
Tap the organ that stores urine before it passes into the urethra.
Tap the hollow organ that expands as it fills with urine.
Tap the organ located between the ureters and the urethra.
Tap the organ that holds urine after it leaves the kidneys and before it leaves the body.

questions.why: The urinary bladder is the hollow, muscular organ that stores urine received from the ureters until it is released through the urethra.
questions.deep: Urine pathway: kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra → outside. The ureters are the thin tubes entering the bladder from above, and the urethra is the single tube leaving it. The bladder wall is smooth muscle that stretches as it fills.

variants.stem: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
Which vessels have thick, muscular walls to withstand the high pressure produced by the heart?
The aorta is the largest example of which type of blood vessel?
Which type of vessel delivers blood from the heart toward the tissues?
Which vessels branch into arterioles and then into capillary beds?
Which blood vessels are associated with the pulse felt at the wrist and neck?
The pulmonary trunk and the aorta are both examples of which category of blood vessel?
Which vessels operate under the highest blood pressure?

questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, elastic, muscular walls because they handle the high pressure of each heartbeat.
questions.deep: Artery = Away from the heart (both start with A). Veins return blood to the heart and have valves and thinner walls. Capillaries are one cell thick and are where exchange of gases and nutrients occurs. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood, so oxygen content does not define an artery.

variants.stem: Which enzyme unwinds DNA and breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs at the start of replication?
Replication begins at an origin where an enzyme separates the two DNA strands. Which enzyme is this?
Which enzyme creates the replication fork by splitting the DNA double helix?
Which enzyme breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases?
Before new strands can be built, which enzyme unzips the DNA double helix?
The A–T base pairs split first during replication because they have only two hydrogen bonds. Which enzyme does the splitting?
Which enzyme is responsible for unwinding the parent DNA molecule at the replication fork?
Which enzyme acts first in DNA replication by deforming the hydrogen bonds between bases?

questions.why: Helicase unwinds the double helix at the origin of replication by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, forming the replication fork.
questions.deep: A–T pairs have two hydrogen bonds; C–G pairs have three, so A–T regions separate more easily. After helicase unwinds the DNA, DNA polymerase builds the new complementary strands, and ligase seals gaps. Memory aid: HELicase = unwinds like a HELix opener.

variants.stem: Where does a substrate bind on an enzyme?
Which region of an enzyme matches the shape of its substrate, explaining the key-in-lock analogy?
What is the name of the region of an enzyme where catalysis takes place?
An enzyme only interacts with substrates that match which part of the enzyme?
In the lock-and-key model, which part of the enzyme acts as the lock?
Competitive inhibitors work by blocking which region of an enzyme?
Which region of an enzyme is highly selective for only certain reactants?
Where does the chemical reaction occur on an enzyme molecule?

questions.why: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site, a region whose shape matches only certain substrates, which is why enzymes are highly selective.
questions.deep: Enzymes are proteins that speed reactions by lowering activation energy. The enzyme may reshape slightly to fit the substrate (induced fit), then release the products and return to its original shape. High temperature or extreme pH can denature an enzyme and destroy its active site.

variants.stem: Which organelle is the main site of ATP production in a cell?
Known as the powerhouse of the cell, which organelle produces most of the cell's ATP?
Cells with a high energy demand, such as muscle cells, contain many of which organelle?
Which organelle has a double membrane and carries out aerobic cellular respiration?
Which organelle contains its own DNA and converts the energy in glucose into ATP?
Oxygen is used to release energy from food in which organelle?
Which organelle's inner folds, called cristae, increase surface area for energy production?
Which structure converts the energy stored in glucose into usable ATP?

questions.why: Mitochondria carry out aerobic cellular respiration and produce most of the cell's ATP.
questions.deep: Mitochondria have a double membrane, an inner membrane folded into cristae, and their own circular DNA; they self-replicate. Ribosomes build proteins, the Golgi modifies and packages them, and lysosomes digest waste.

variants.stem: During which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes line up along the cell's equator?
Which phase of mitosis is when the chromosomes are arranged in a single line across the middle of the cell?
Spindle fibers attached to the centromeres hold the chromosomes at the center of the cell. Which phase is this?
Which phase comes right before sister chromatids are pulled apart toward opposite poles?
In which phase of mitosis are the chromosomes at the equatorial plane?
Which phase follows prophase and precedes anaphase?
A cell biologist sees all of the chromosomes lined up at the center of the cell. Which phase of mitosis is this?
The metaphase plate forms during which stage of mitosis?

questions.why: During metaphase, the chromosomes line up at the cell's equator (the metaphase plate), attached to spindle fibers.
questions.deep: Mitosis order: prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope breaks down) → metaphase (chromosomes line up in the middle) → anaphase (sister chromatids pulled apart) → telophase (two nuclei re-form), then cytokinesis. Memory aid: Metaphase = Middle.

variants.stem: Why can't a virus reproduce on its own?
opts: It lacks the machinery to replicate without a host cell
It is too large to divide
It is made only of cytoplasm

variants.stem: Which statement about viruses is true?
opts: They can replicate only inside a host cell
They carry out their own metabolism

variants.stem: A virus must infect another cell in order to:
Viruses are called obligate intracellular parasites. What does this mean?
opts: They can reproduce only inside host cells
They can live and grow in any nonliving environment

variants.stem: How do viruses reproduce?
opts: By taking over a host cell's machinery

variants.stem: Which feature makes viruses dependent on living cells?
opts: They lack their own machinery for making proteins

variants.stem: In the life cycle of a virus, the host cell provides the:
opts: Machinery needed to make new viral parts

variants.stem: A bacteriophage infects a bacterium and uses it to make more phages. This shows that viruses require:

questions.why: Viruses have genetic material and a protein coat but no machinery of their own for making proteins or energy, so they can replicate only by taking over a host cell.
questions.deep: A virus's life cycle: attach to host cell → enter → host cell makes viral parts → assemble → release. Bacteria are living cells that reproduce on their own by binary fission, which is why antibiotics work on bacteria but not viruses.

variants.stem: In a balanced chemical equation, what must be true?
opts: The number of each type of atom is the same on both sides
The number of molecules is the same on both sides

variants.stem: The Law of Conservation of Mass states that in a chemical reaction:
opts: Matter is neither created nor destroyed
Atoms are changed into new elements

variants.stem: Why must chemical equations be balanced?
opts: Matter cannot be created or destroyed

variants.stem: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is a balanced equation because:
opts: Each side has the same number of H and O atoms
Each side has the same number of molecules
The subscripts match on both sides
Oxygen is on the left only

variants.stem: Ten grams of reactants are sealed in a closed container and react completely. What is the total mass of the products?
Which principle explains why the atoms on the reactant side of an equation equal the atoms on the product side?
In any chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants compared with the total mass of the products is:
A chemist balances an equation by changing coefficients. Which rule does this satisfy?

questions.why: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so a balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides.
questions.deep: Balance equations by changing coefficients (the numbers in front of formulas), never subscripts, which would change the substances. Five basic reaction types: combination, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion.

variants.stem: An object has a mass of 50 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
A metal sample weighs 50 grams and occupies 20 cubic centimeters. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
Find the density, in g/cm³, of a substance with a mass of 50 g and a volume of 20 mL.
A block of material has a volume of 20 cm³ and a mass of 50 g. What is the density, in g/cm³?
Calculate the density in g/cm³ of a liquid if 20 cm³ of it has a mass of 50 g.
A student measures an unknown solid: mass = 50 g, volume = 20 cm³. What is the density in g/cm³?
What is the density, in grams per cubic centimeter, of a rock that has a mass of 50 g and takes up 20 cm³?
Using density = mass ÷ volume, find the density in g/cm³ of a sample with mass 50 g and volume 20 cm³.

questions.why: Density = mass ÷ volume = 50 g ÷ 20 cm³ = 2.5 g/cm³.
questions.deep: Water's density is about 1 g/cm³, so anything denser than 1 g/cm³ sinks in water if it is solid and uniform. Remember 1 mL = 1 cm³. An object's overall density includes any air inside it, which is why a hollow steel ship can float.

variants.stem: What does molarity (M) measure?
opts: Moles of solute per liter of solution
Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Grams of solute per liter of solvent
Moles of solvent per liter of solution

variants.stem: A 1.0 M solution contains 1.0 mole of solute in each ____ of solution.
Which expression defines molarity?
opts: Moles of solute ÷ liters of solution
Moles of solute ÷ kilograms of solvent
Grams of solute ÷ liters of solvent
Moles of solvent ÷ liters of solution

variants.stem: Molarity differs from molality because molarity is based on the amount of:
Which unit is used to express the concentration of a solution as molarity?
Which concentration measure compares the moles of solute with the volume of the entire solution?
The concentration of a solution expressed in mol/L is called its:
To calculate molarity, which two quantities are needed?
opts: Moles of solute and liters of solution
Moles of solvent and mass of solution
Grams of solvent and liters of solute
Volume of solute and mass of solvent

questions.why: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L).
questions.deep: Molality (m) is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. To find moles from grams, divide grams of solute by its molar mass. For dilutions use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. A 1.0 M solution is more concentrated than a 0.1 M solution.

variants.stem: What makes an acid "strong"?
opts: It ionizes almost completely in solution

variants.stem: Which describes a strong acid in water?
opts: Nearly all of its molecules ionize
Only a few of its molecules ionize

variants.stem: The strength of an acid reflects the degree to which it:
HCl is a strong acid. What does this tell you about HCl in water?
opts: Only a little of it ionizes

variants.stem: Highly reactive acids in which most of the molecules ionize are classified as:
Which statement about a strong acid is correct?
opts: It always has a higher pH than a weak acid

variants.stem: In a solution of a strong acid, which is true of the acid molecules?
Acid strength depends on how completely an acid does what in water?

questions.why: A strong acid ionizes (dissociates) almost completely in water, while a weak acid only partly ionizes.
questions.deep: Strong acids include HCl, H₂SO₄, and HNO₃; acetic acid (in vinegar) is a weak acid. Strength is different from concentration: you can have a dilute solution of a strong acid or a concentrated solution of a weak acid. Strong acids have lower pH at the same concentration.

variants.stem: Which type of bond forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons?
Water molecules contain hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined by which type of bond?
The sharing of electron pairs between two nonmetal atoms produces which type of bond?
Which bond results from an attraction caused by the sharing of electrons between atoms?
In O₂, the two oxygen atoms share electrons. What type of bond joins them?
Which bond is formed within a CH₄ molecule between carbon and hydrogen?
Which type of bond is characterized by shared electron pairs rather than transferred electrons?
Two nonmetal atoms with similar electronegativities that bond with each other will most likely form which type of bond?

questions.why: A covalent bond forms when atoms, usually nonmetals, share one or more pairs of electrons.
questions.deep: Ionic bond = electrons transferred (metal + nonmetal). Covalent bond = electrons shared (nonmetal + nonmetal). If the sharing is unequal (different electronegativity), the bond is polar covalent, as in water. Hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between molecules, not bonds inside them.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which of the following are chemical changes?
Select all that apply: Which of these are physical changes?
Select all that apply: In which of these does a new substance form?
Select all that apply: Which changes involve only a change in state or form, not a new substance?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are chemical changes?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are physical changes?
Select all that apply: Which processes change the chemical composition of a substance?
Select all that apply: Which processes do NOT change the chemical identity of the substance?

questions.why: A chemical change forms new substances (burning, rusting, digesting, rotting), while a physical change alters only state, shape, or size (melting, freezing, boiling, dissolving, cutting).
questions.deep: Signs of a chemical change: gas given off, color change, light or heat released, a precipitate forming. Changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation) are physical changes because the substance's identity stays the same.

variants.stem: How should the volume of a liquid in a graduated cylinder be read?
opts: At eye level, from the bottom of the curved surface
From above, at the top of the curved surface
From below, at the top of the curved surface
At arm's length, at the edge of the glass

variants.stem: The surface of a liquid in a graduated cylinder forms a curve called a meniscus. Where should the measurement be taken?
opts: At the bottom of the curve
At the top of the curve
At the edge touching the glass
At the middle of the cylinder

variants.stem: To avoid reading errors with a graduated cylinder, the observer should:
opts: Read at eye level on a flat surface
Hold the cylinder in one hand and look from above
Look from above to see the top edge
Read the number nearest the rim

variants.stem: A student reads a graduated cylinder from above and records the top of the meniscus. What should have been done instead?
opts: Read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
Read from above at the top of the meniscus
Read from below at the glass edge

variants.stem: Which procedure gives the most accurate reading of a liquid volume in a graduated cylinder?
opts: Place it on a flat surface and read the meniscus at eye level
Hold it at an angle and read the rim
Tilt it slightly and read the top
Read it from above the level of the eyes

variants.stem: Which point on the lens-shaped liquid surface is used when measuring volume in a graduated cylinder?
Where should your eyes be in relation to the liquid surface when reading a graduated cylinder?
A liquid in a graduated cylinder has a curved surface. The correct reading is the volume at the:

questions.why: Place the cylinder on a flat surface and read it at eye level, taking the measurement from the bottom of the curved liquid surface (the meniscus).
questions.deep: Graduated cylinders are more precise than beakers and Erlenmeyer flasks but less precise than volumetric flasks or pipettes. Reading from above or below causes parallax error. For water-based liquids the meniscus curves downward, so read the lowest point.

variants.stem: Convert 450 milligrams to grams.
A tablet contains 450 mg of an ingredient. How many grams is that?
A sample has a mass of 450 mg. What is its mass in grams?
How many grams are in 450 mg?
A lab technician weighs 450 milligrams of a powder. Express this mass in grams.
Using metric prefixes, convert 450 mg to g.
A chemical has a mass of 450 mg. Give its mass in g.
Express 450 mg in grams.

questions.why: Milli- means one thousandth, so 1 g = 1000 mg and 450 mg ÷ 1000 = 0.45 g.
questions.deep: To convert from a smaller unit to a larger one, divide; to go from larger to smaller, multiply. Moving the decimal point 3 places to the left converts mg to g. Prefix order: kilo, hecto, deka, (base unit), deci, centi, milli.

variants.stem: In an experiment, which term describes the variables that are kept the same for all groups?
A student tests how temperature affects how much sugar dissolves in water. The type of solvent, the amount of stirring, and the pressure are kept the same. What are these called?
Which type of variable should be carefully controlled so it does not change during an experiment?
Factors such as pot size, soil type, and amount of water that are the same for every plant in an experiment are called:
Why are constants important in an experiment?
opts: They keep other factors from affecting the results
They are the variable being measured
They are the variable being changed
They are the prediction being tested

variants.stem: All variables other than the independent and dependent variables should be treated as:
Which of the following are variables that a researcher deliberately holds the same across trials?
In an experiment, the variables that are not tested and are kept unchanged are known as:

questions.why: Constants are the variables deliberately kept the same in every group so that only the independent variable affects the results.
questions.deep: Only one variable (the independent or manipulated variable) is purposely changed. The dependent (responding) variable is observed and recorded. Everything else should be a constant, otherwise you cannot tell what caused any change in the results.
